title: Laurena Diggs and Carrie Boote Interview, 1959-05-25

pages.label: 001_Laurena Diggs and Carrie Boote Interview, 1959-05-25 Part 1

blocks.x: Right ahead, Paul. Okay, well, I'll put my name on that first to show you what I'm on. My name is Dick Allen. Paul? Paul Crawford.
Lorena Diggs. And Carrie Diggs Boot.
Carrie Diggs Boot. Uh-huh. Okay, well, we'll keep y'all straight. I'll call you Ms. Diggs and you and Ms. Boot.
Yeah.
Okay, all right. So, Ms. Diggs, when were you born?
When?
Yes.
In October 18 and 73 in Mobile, Alabama.
And, uh, let's see now. You grew up in Mobile?
Grew up in Mobile till I was...

pages.label: 002_Laurena Diggs and Carrie Boote Interview, 1959-05-25 Part 2

blocks.x: When you're ready, just go ahead. You want to tell about that clipping? Oh, this? Yellow fever?

Well, I said that the... That was in May when... Well, all that I can say, I remember that time and date, you know, in 1878, when the yellow people were so bad that the trains wasn't... The bells wasn't ringing on the steam cars and the town was all quiet. No bells or whatsoever. The people were dying three and four into the homes. And I visited family one day, went back the next day to play with my little comrades and they were all dead. They were white right at the corner. Good children, we called it.

pages.label: 003_Laurena Diggs and Carrie Boote Interview, 1959-05-25 Part 3

blocks.x: You were saying about Jones at the Royal College.
Yeah, he's called Professor Jones. I see. He was emcee there for years.
And who was in the band there?

Well, now, they had Lil Armstrong. She wasn't a Lil Armstrong then. I don't know what her name, but later on she married Louis. And King Oliver had the band there then. And Louis was on the, I should say the second trumpet, because King Oliver played the, you know, he was on the first trumpet, I guess. I don't know where they're placed in the band, but King Oliver and Lil, she were at the piano. That's where her and Louis met. I don't know if they met there, but I mean they worked together and they married from there. Because she's from St. Louis and I didn't know her maiden name, but I know she was playing the piano with King Oliver during the time that they were at the Royal Court.
Did you know any of the other fellas in the band?

Oh, now, I know Louis. And then, I did know a fella named Freddie, Freddie Hall. He played the drums. He's from here, big stuff, Tubby. You heard of Tubby? Yeah, sure. Well, I remember Tubby. And another boy, his name is, he played the, he's from here. Now, what is his name? Oh, let me see. He plays in some of the leading bands. Now, I don't, I can't remember his name just now, but I remember Tubby, and I remember Lil, and Louis, and Oliver. Those are all I can remember right now that were in the band at that time.
Before the tape machine was on, you mentioned this fella, Kepler?
Freddie? Freddie Kepler. Well, I didn't know of any band he had. I just know that he played good connect, and I know he used to play around Chicago. Oh, yeah. Uh-huh.
But you didn't know him personally?
I just knew of him, not no close associates. I just know he played around Chicago.
I was going to ask you where some of the best bands played in New Orleans. What would be some of the halls and places like that?

What do you mean? Here in New Orleans? Uh-huh. Well, now, during the time I lived here, I didn't go out very much to very many dances, because now, they used to have a dance place up here on Danille Street they called a Palm Garden, and this Buddy P.T. It wasn't Buddy P.T. He had a band there, but I didn't go very often, but I went up there once or twice. He had a band there. Now, this Arobishow, it seemed like to me he played at St. Catherine Hall. And then, uh, on the Ruth Garden, I can't remember what this man's name is, but later years, he used to try to produce shows, because he sent a girl from here named Vivian Segu to Chicago. He was like a booking agency, but he had a band on the Ruth Garden during that time. See, I didn't get out to very many dances here. I just, you know, knew other bands, but I didn't go. But I know Buddy P.T., he used to play up here at the Palm Garden, and, uh, and Kid Ory, he used to play right over here sometime. And this, uh, it was the Bulls then. It wasn't the, uh, Elks. Elks, it was the Bulls Club. Oh, the Bulls used to play with them. Oh, they, well, the, at, when different affairs, they would have different bands. That wasn't a regular place, just like a nightclub. They just had bands and whatever band they felt like kind, they would have them, but...
Let's get the address down here. This is 1926 Harmony.
Yeah, 1926 Harmony.
And I can look right out the window and see the Bulls. Yeah. Now the Elks.
It's the Elks now. Mm-hmm. But at that time, it used to be the Bulls.
And this is May the 25th, 1959. Did they have the dances and the Bulls inside or outside?

They, they had, uh, dances downstairs, and then they used to have them in that yard. Oh, I see. Uh-huh. They have a paved yard there. And they used to have dances in that yard. Uh-huh. Do you know any of the bands that were there?
At the Bulls very much other than Owey?
No, I didn't know any of the bands there because, you know, soon after that I left and then it went on and on.
Would they draw a bigger crowd in Chicago or a smaller one? Would the dance halls be bigger up there or smaller?
Oh, the dance, well they have the, they did have the Savoy Ballroom. Mm-hmm. But the dances seemed like they, they'd be larger there because it's more people and the halls are larger.
That's why I look everywhere.
Do you remember any of the other people in Olle Powell's band?

Oh, let me see now. The only person I knew was Olle, and I knew, um, this Glover played piano. And, um, let's see, that's been way back in 1920. You kind of forget, you know, when they, when you, I can't think of anyone just now.
What about Tony Jackson? Did you ever know him around Chicago or here?
Tony Jackson.
He was a piano player. Tony Jackson. He wrote Pretty Baby. Yeah.
No, I, I, I, I don't remember Tony Jackson. I can't remember him. He didn't play in any of the leading bands around there.
Well, I think he was mostly, uh, just a piano player.
A soloist player to himself. No, I don't, uh, remember him because most of the bands around Chicago, I mostly knew of, you know, by way. You know, by working around there. Because, uh,
What about, uh, Tommy Ladinier? Did you ever know him in Chicago?
Tommy Ladinier.
He was from down here. In Mandeville. I thought maybe you knew him.

No. Well, you know, most, if they were connected with any, any of the bands around there, mostly I would know them. But a lot of those, uh, piano players, now, they had a fellow here named Peg Gauman. Gauman. Gauman. He was a colored fellow, but he always passed, and he played down in the district here. Now, he left here, and he went to Chicago. But he, he passed for White, and he played with the orchestra at the Chicago Theater for years. And, of course, he was a very good piano player. But by him going there, and getting out of circulation, and went on the north side, well, we, we never knew anything about him. But he was a boyfriend of my cousin's, and actually I knew him for years from being associated with her. But he played now at the Chicago Theater for years. Peck Gauman. He used to play in the, on Bourbon Street, Peck, played piano. Very handsome fellow. And, uh, and you see, when you go there, and if you get on the north side, in any of those places, just with a small band, uh, uh, and, and a lot of those colored fellows, when they go there, they, like their solo band, like their solo piano player, they play and sing between times, just like when the big band start playing, then you, they have a small little piano, and then you, it's like a little, uh, on a flat phone. You know, just a tiny piano. But after the dance is over, you get, um, this little piano, and you can push it from one table to the other, around the, uh, the dance floor, and if you have a party here, and anything you want to hear, well, I sing it for you, and then the other, and they go around. But once, when you get over there, you're just out of circulation with the public. You know, you're all right over on the north side, but just like most of the colored people on the south side, they wouldn't know what's happening, you know, in these other places. Because, now, you're welcome to go if you want to, but they have all the fun they want in their own neighborhood, and they'd very seldom go over there. Well, now, so many of the boys have went over there, and they got popular financially, but they are not known because they do this solo way by themselves. Now, they have a boy, he isn't, uh, uh, from here, he, he worked with Punch, Fred Reed. Now, he, uh, plays piano, and before they were making this big money, he was making around $500 a week. But he was a very fine piano player. He's from Jackson, Mississippi, but he played with all the Louisiana boys, and everybody thought he was from New Orleans. Now, he plays by himself. You know, after the orchestra plays, he and the teams. And the women just come from all over just to hear him sing and play. Fred Reed is his name. And, uh, but nobody knows him on the south side as a great pianist, because he's over there in this white cabaret, and he's making his money. And, uh, the being popular among the other people don't mean nothing. Financials, you know, is what he was interested in. But he played with Punch and, uh, Francois for a while, and then when he went there, well, people have forgotten about Fred no more, and they know about the buildings. He's buying a car or something like that, but his sister and I are very good friends, and she said that his salary is $500 a week. And, uh, I don't know if that has anything to do with tips or anything, because when some of them, they call you to play, they may hand you $5 or $10. Some of this weak women, they hand you $5 now. Now, you take Punch. He used to, uh, sing, You Got Me Between the Devil and the Deep Blue Sea, and he used to sing Marie. And my phone would ring off the walls when he would broadcast, you know, on the radio, sing, and he was very popular at that time, you know. And, uh, just, him singing made him so popular, but that's the way it was with Fred. When he got over there, the women seemed to like his playing and his voice, and he just buried himself there, and he's doing very well financially.
You said your phone would ring one.

No, I was talking about the different people when they found where Punch was living at. They would ring, he, he roomed with me, you know. And I said different women, white and colored would call it. I had to put a very rich woman out of my home. He can tell you about his, uh, singing. She came there with her chauffeur and all. And Punch can tell you I had to ask her out. And she wanted Punch to sing, and just, because at that time I wasn't broad enough to understand, but she just wanted to hear him sing. She said no harm, she said. That was her pleasure, and her husband had her chauffeur to take her anywhere she wanted to go, and she paid for whatever she wanted. But I didn't care to be bothered, and I wouldn't allow her to come in. Punch can tell you. And they, and she, he, they would call night and day for Punch. Punch had a very good voice before he, he made records too, you know. And he did pretty good, but it just seemed like some people gets to the top, they have more business abilities, and some don't. And then when you have a good manager, Joe Glazer wanted Punch once, but, uh, you know, Punch, Joe, they want so much, and this thing and the other. And he had nobody told him just how to go about, and he wouldn't go on, but if he had went with Joe Glazer, maybe he would have been, you know, popular today. But he thought it was bad not to.
Did you have a phonograph in those days?
Huh?
Did you have a phonograph yourself of Victrola?

Oh, yeah, yeah. Uh-huh. I have, uh, oh, I have a collection of records in Chicago. I still have my house in Chicago. I got all Bessie Smith, Manny Smith, Clara Smith, I got all her records. I, I'm sure I have some of Punch's records. I, I don't know, but I have, uh, a lot of old records that I had just put in the box and put aside as I get new ones. I have some old records, I guess, 25 or 30 some years old there. Please come out. I got to see that.
Yeah. I was there, and I know what some of them when I was there had.

Yeah, I have, uh, boxes of records. I, we had a phonograph since 1920. We got, we had one here. Mm-hmm. And then when I went to Chicago, I, I, is there, every, my thing improved? I improved with it. I had one of those that you turn, you know how you turn. Mm-hmm. And when the other electric came out, I had one of those.
Yeah, I hope you have a ton of these. What, uh, kind of recordings did people like down in their 20s? Remember what that was called?

Well, now, I think, uh, a lot of people, they, well, it's, um, now, like blues and some don't, but blues went pretty good during the 20s, you know? Because, just like the records they made, now, Bessie Smith and Mamie Smith, uh, Trixie, uh, Chippy Hill, and, uh, Sarah Martin, all those were old blues singers, and they were top record, uh, artists during those years. So, they must have undoubtedly liked blues during that time, see? Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Because, I, I kind of think they, they like, they like, as far as the records part, they like blues. Mm-hmm. Those are all women. Huh? Those are all women that you named.
Yeah, but, uh, the men weren't doing much record making during that time. Mm-hmm.

Those are all women that, uh, they weren't, uh, they weren't, you know, you know how his records, they were talking records and things like that. But, they didn't have very many, uh, men recording during, to my knowing, during that time. They mostly had, uh, women.
Do you remember what was the first band record you ever heard?

Well, now, the first band record, let me see, uh, the first music that I ever remember playing, I don't know, Victrola, was by Mamie Smith. Now, what band that accompanied her, I don't know, because that was a band out east. But, that was the first, uh, uh, band that I, uh, remember. King Oliver with the Diplomouth. Wasn't it the Diplomouth? Mm-hmm. And, uh, Louis played, had a Savoy. Those are some of the early records that I remembered. And, that was in, uh, around 1923 or 1922. Somewhere around in there. I mean, the Diplomouth. And, then, they had something they called High Society. They had, uh, King Oliver did that. High Society and the Diplomouth. And, uh, Louis, he had the Savoy. And, oh, quite a few records. But, I think, uh, King Oliver's was about the first that I remember hearing, because he recorded before Louis did. King Oliver did. And, I'm, I'm not sure, but I don't know if Louis played with him during his making of that record or not. He may have, but I can't say. But, I remember that's about the first dance record that I remember was King Oliver's record. And, that was in the early 20s. But, I never knew too many men to make records during that time. Most of them were women, you know, until later years.
I'm sort of jumping around today, but, uh, you say you had piano teachers? Did you have a voice teacher, too?

Me? No, no. Just, what little I tried was just something I, you know. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. they used to have organ grinders, you know, going around the street and you put the nickel and the man would play your piece. Well, most children save their nickels, you know, and when he'd come around, they'd get out there and dance up a breeze right on the street, you know. And there are so many children and so many people here. Years ago, if you wanted a piano player, you didn't have to go look all around. You could look out and see most anybody could hit a tune and didn't know a word of music. Now, just like this Steve Lewis, I don't think he knew music and he played all down, I don't know what this, some white club, West End, isn't it West End here? Well, he played down there in the ten of the years and he didn't know anything about reading music, but he could play anything you asked him to, see. Well, now, during that time, that man would play the organ. Sometimes they had a monkey, you know, would go around and pick up the things and the kids would get out on the sidewalk and just like the dance, you know, behind the band and have fun dancing out in the street. Well, that was when I was small, you know. And then they used to have amateur night. Clarence Williams and Edith Taylor, I think that's his wife, they used to have amateur nights. They had a show round up in here. I don't know where it is. Where was it? Where Prince Goodwood Hospital is. Yeah, I forgot. But you see, you would get on this amateur, you know, and a lot of people just would take up from singing and dancing out in the street. And then if they think they got good, they'd get on amateur night and you'd dance there. You may have went on a week engagement at the Regal or something like that. And a lot of people just went on from that. And just late years, people really worried about voice culture and theatrical. Well, in the early 20s, you just went on and got up there and sing. And went on dancing. They didn't call it tap dancing. They called it buck dancing, you know. And you could just get out there and cut a step and look like, just like in a course, they had somebody to show you the step all right. But if you didn't have eye enough to just catch on, you was lost. Nobody taking time, you know. They had someone to train you. But in the meantime, you caught on. You should know something about it without a teacher. So when any time you went to this, worked in a nightclub, you'd stand there and look a while and fall in line. And you'd start stumbling off with something. And it went right along. Because I know some of the leading, just like Ethel Waters. Ethel Waters, she worked in a street fair with a fellow named James Seymour. It used to be Jeanette and Seymour. They were a very popular team. And Neoma Brown and McGraw. You heard of Brown and McGraw?
No, I haven't.
Well, she was a colored girl from here. She looked like an Indian looking girl. But she, Paul Ash, they were the leading couple. You remember Paul Ash?
No, I'm afraid this is new to me.

Paul Ash was a great white band in Chicago. Oh, I have heard of the band. Yeah. Well, now, she was his leading lady in this all-white band. But she never had a lesson of nothing. Her and this Brown just got to dancing among themselves and got up the team. And they was one of the country's top dancers during that time, Brown and McGraw.
Which is which?

Her name is Naomi McGraw, and his name was Herbert Brown. And they had McKinney's cotton pickers. She had, they hired them to travel with her. Naomi and McGraw. She's right from here. Now, here, and they never had any dancing instruction. All they did was take up dancing themselves right here out on the street. That's what they told me now. And, boy, as I know, I never known them to do. Their music and excitement here has a lot to do with some of the, well, I think just New Orleans is a great town for entertainment. And there's so many of the people that's made good, if you hear them being interviewed, they say they got a lot of their experience right off the street. From dancing and jigging and watching other people. And they give up something and go right on. Well, because this Herbert Brown, he was a great dancer. He paid some years, but he worked with, on the office cycle, the best, you know, that's the largest cycle for vaudeville actress. And he never was out of work unless they wanted to be. And some of the greatest dancers in the olden times, they never had dancing lessons. They just took it up and went on and danced.
Did you say that you worked, that you were on the stage around here before you went to Chicago?
Just in a ragtime, see, they didn't call it a minstrel. Minstrel, it was a ragtime concert, but you went through the same performance, you know.
I was wondering, did you know any of the organ grinders? Who they'd be?
They were all white fellas. They didn't have no colored idol. They used to have little monkeys, you know. And when they'd get ready, he'd come out with a little cup. You never heard of them?
Oh, sure, but there was one colored guy that did, and I'm trying to think of his name.

Well, I don't remember any colored, but I know these white, they used to come around and, you know, the children would save their nickels for it. And they'd get out and dance with each other. And then during that time, they had, like, they call it talent night, but amateur night, you know. And if you had a play in your backyard, you'd get out there and brush your heels out there dancing in order to get on this, you know, amateur night to see what you could do. Well, nobody instructed you. You just got out there and danced, and then if you made good, you just went from there.
Did they have a band or a piano there for when you were trying out?

Oh, yeah. This, at the Lyric, they had a Robichaux's band when they used to have amateur night at the Regal. And Clarence Williams used to have a band here. Clarence Williams, now. Yeah, yeah, he had a wife named Edith Taylor. He was a songwriter. Yeah, that's the same one. He used to have a little band here, Clarence. Sure, yeah. That was on the AMA two nights.
Don't you have that left phone? You want to cook over? Yeah, I think I'm playing food. Oh, you didn't tell us about your education any time. I think you left off.

Well, I attended public school in Morris Point, Mississippi, and then I attended Miller's Ferranormal Industrial School. And then, in the later years, I finished a course at the Roosevelt College in Chicago of Public Speaking. And in 1946, I finished a course at the University of Wisconsin. And then, from the University of Wisconsin, I went to the University of Chicago. And in the later years, I was a member. Wait, I've got the papers to show you. A member of the executive board.
